title: Rust Foundations: Ownership to a Safe Persistent Tracker
description: A beginner Rust course covering Cargo, types, Option, Result, patterns, ownership, borrowing, collections, structs, enums, traits, file errors, threads, channels, and a tested capstone.
prerequisites: Ability to create and save a text file
learningOutcomes: Build, format, lint, diagnose, and test Rust crates
Use explicit result types, patterns, ownership, borrowing, collections, structs, enums, and traits
Build a persistent tracker with validated state, contextual errors, safe concurrency, and tests

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Cargo manages Rust packages, called crates. `cargo new` creates a package, `cargo fmt` applies standard formatting, `cargo check` performs fast type and borrow checking, `cargo test` runs tests, and `cargo run` builds and executes a binary. `Cargo.toml` records package metadata and dependencies; `Cargo.lock` records resolved versions for reproducible application builds. Rust compiler diagnostics often include source spans and suggestions, but understand the violated rule before applying a fix. Run Clippy to identify suspicious or unnecessarily complex code.

objectives: Explain and apply Types, Parsing, Option, and Result

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Bindings are immutable unless declared `mut`. Rust infers many local types but public contracts should remain clear. Tuples and arrays have fixed shape; `String` owns growable UTF-8 text while `&str` is a borrowed string slice. Parsing returns `Result`, so success and failure must be handled. `Option<T>` represents a value that may be absent without using null. Match both variants or use combinators when they remain readable. The `?` operator returns an error to the caller after conversion; it does not ignore failure.

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: `if` is an expression whose branches must produce compatible types. `match` must be exhaustive and can destructure enums, tuples, and structs while applying guards. Use `if let` when one pattern is important and other cases can be ignored intentionally. Rust provides `loop`, `while`, and `for`; ranges such as `0..n` exclude the upper bound. Iterator adapters are lazy until consumed. Choose direct control flow over dense chains when it makes failure and boundaries easier to review.

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Each Rust value has an owner and is dropped when that owner leaves scope. Assignment of a non-Copy value usually moves ownership, preventing accidental double use. A shared reference `&T` permits reading; an exclusive reference `&mut T` permits mutation, and their active use cannot conflict. References must never outlive the data they borrow. Slices borrow contiguous regions without ownership. `Vec<T>` owns a growable sequence, but pushing may reallocate and invalidate element references, so keep borrows short. HashMap lookup returns an Option.

lessons.summary: Design domain models with typed functions, structs, impl blocks, enums, traits, generics, visibility, and invariant-preserving constructors.
objectives: Explain and apply Functions, Structs, Enums, and Traits
Use compiler, lint, and test evidence to verify behavior

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Functions declare parameter and return types. Structs model related data, enums model a value that is exactly one of several variants, and methods live in `impl` blocks. Keep fields private when arbitrary mutation could violate invariants. A constructor conventionally named `new` can return `Result<Self, Error>` when validation may fail. Traits define shared behavior and are implemented explicitly. Generic bounds state required capabilities. Prefer enums over boolean combinations for meaningful states, because exhaustive matching keeps transitions visible.

lessons.title: Files, Serialization, Threads, and a Tracker
lessons.summary: Combine validated models, file errors, serialization boundaries, threads or channels, shared ownership, synchronization, and tests in a persistent tracker.
objectives: Explain and apply Files, Serialization, Threads, and a Tracker

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: File operations return `Result` and should add path and operation context while preserving the source error. Deserialized data is untrusted and must pass domain constructors before becoming application state. Threads require transferred values to satisfy lifetime and thread-safety rules; `move` closures transfer captured ownership. Channels support message passing. Shared mutable state commonly uses `Arc<Mutex<T>>`; handle poisoned locks deliberately and keep critical sections short. Join worker threads and propagate failures instead of allowing detached work to outlive the operation.

finalAssessment.instructionsMarkdown: Build a Rust progress tracker using private validated models, enums, Result-based contextual errors, borrowed interfaces, safe persistence, bounded thread or channel lifecycles, synchronized state where necessary, and at least ten automated tests.
